title: Who am I?
hook: Ramana Maharshi taught self-enquiry: ask "who am I?" and trace the "I" to its source

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was kirtan: one voice calls, the room answers, singing the names. Your line was call and response.

A clinic intake form asks who you are, in pieces. Name. Address. Occupation. Emergency contact. Allergies. Each box is small, and each answer is true. Fill them all in and you've described a person well enough to be treated, billed and called back. In South India, at the foot of a hill called Arunachala, a quiet teacher named Ramana Maharshi asked the same question with no boxes at all. He didn't want it filled in. He wanted it followed, the way you'd follow a stream uphill to see where it starts.
screen: `AN INTAKE FORM, IN PIECES.` → `A HILL CALLED ARUNACHALA.` → `FOLLOWED, NOT FILLED IN.`

segments.voice: Ramana's teaching survives in short works and in conversations his visitors wrote down. One small booklet carries the question as its title: in Tamil, Nan Yar, who am I? This is a paraphrase, not his words, but the method goes like this. Every thought you have is somebody's thought. Before the worry, before the plan, there is an I that has it. In Ramana's account, that sense of I is the first thought, and every other thought rises after it. So when a thought comes, don't follow it out into the world. Turn it around: to whom did this come? To me. And who am I? Not a riddle to solve with words. Ramana goes through the obvious answers: not the body, not the senses, not even the thinking mind. One way readers put it: each of these can be noticed, and the I is the one noticing. The point is to keep attention on the I itself, and trace it back toward where it rises. He gives a striking picture for what the question does. At a cremation, someone stirs the fire with a stick, keeping it burning. At the end, the stick goes into the fire too. The question works on all the other thoughts like that stick, he says, and in the end it burns up as well. Then the asking stops, and what remains is not another thought. Yesterday a room sang names. Today, a single word, I, followed home.
screen: `EVERY THOUGHT IS SOMEBODY'S.` · `TO WHOM DID THIS COME?` · `NOT THE BODY, NOT THE MIND.` · `THE STICK THAT STIRS THE FIRE.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Ask "who am I?" once, inside, slowly, and wait without answering in words; if an answer shows up anyway, a job, a name, a mood, ask: to whom did this come? Ask again with a longer silence, and a third time with the longest silence of all. You're not looking for a reply, only at where the question lands.
Who am I? Ramana Maharshi's self-enquiry: meet each thought by asking to whom it came, and follow the I back to its source. Today's word.
Your line: who am I. A question that isn't meant to end in an answer. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: People who follow Ramana Maharshi's teaching practice self-enquiry by meeting each thought with the question "to whom did this come?" and turning attention back to the sense of I, in sitting practice and through the day.
